parakeet: In Matthew's version, the event is attached to a much larger public disruption. That cannot be easily contained inside a chosen witnesses framework. Because now the question is not merely why didn't Jesus appear to everyone. The question becomes: how can an event involving earthquakes, open tombs, multiple resurrected dead people, and public appearances in Jerusalem leave no clear contemporary record? That is a containment problem. A private appearance can be theologically restricted. A civic disruption cannot. A visionary experience can be limited to chosen witnesses. An earthquake can't. A private revelation can be confined to a movement. Open tombs and resurrected people walking into the city cannot be so easily contained. So the apologetic defense creates a contradiction. Apologists want to explain the lack of public evidence by saying Jesus only appeared to chosen witnesses, but the gospel story itself includes public phenomena that would have expanded the witness pool far beyond those chosen few. That's why the chosen witnesses answer does not fully solve the problem. It only answers a smaller version of the claim. It might explain why Jesus didn't appear in Pilate's court at the temple or before Caesar, but it doesn't explain why no one else seems to know about the earthquake, the open tombs, the raised saints, or their appearance to many people in Jerusalem. If the resurrection story were only Jesus appeared privately to selected followers, then the chosen witness argument would at least be internally coherent. But once the narrative includes earthquakes, open graves, multiple resurrections, and appearances to many people inside Jerusalem, the event is no longer containable. The audience has expanded beyond the chosen witnesses. The resurrection cannot be defended as private revelation while being narrated as public disruption. Apologists can't use chosen witnesses to explain away the lack of public evidence for an event their own text describes as publicly disruptive.
